answer: The paper's P/D model holds qualitatively in BLIS and quantitatively at low-to-moderate rates, but breaks down structurally at high rates due to batch size capping. Specifically: (1) The ITL formula ITL=alpha/(1-lambda*W) fits excellently at rates 1-30 (R²>0.999, MAPE<0.08%) and well at rates 1-60 (R²>0.997, MAPE<0.44%), but degrades at rates 1-150 (R²=0.92-0.95, MAPE=2.5-3.9%) with systematic S-shaped residuals, and fails badly at rates 1-400 (R²=0.66-0.73) because ITL approaches a ceiling rather than diverging as M/G/1 predicts. (2) The ceiling mechanism is batch size capping: BLIS's max_num_running_reqs=256 bounds the batch, so step time saturates around 21.4ms (AL) / 20ms (AD) — a 75% increase over baseline, not the infinity M/G/1 predicts. The paper's M/G/1 derivation assumes unbounded batch growth (B=lambda*W*T_iter → infinity as rho→1), which is violated by any practical system with a batch cap. (3) All directional predictions hold at rates 1-150: ITL_AD < ITL_AL at every rate (by 0-1.7ms), TTFT_AD > TTFT_AL (by 4-16ms), and AD has higher capacity (456 vs 395 implied req/s, ratio 1.155). (4) A new finding: the TTFT ordering REVERSES at rate≈250 — beyond this AL TTFT > AD TTFT because AD's isolated prefill pool keeps TTFT nearly constant (49.8ms at all rates) while AL TTFT explodes (119ms at rate=400) due to head-of-line blocking from large decode batches. (5) E2E favors AD at ALL tested rates (1-400) because ITL savings × 128 tokens always exceed the TTFT penalty. (6) Results are essentially deterministic across seeds (max CV = 0.009%). (7) The step time in BLIS is NOT linear in batch size (contrary to the paper's Eq 9 assumption): it depends on the roofline max(compute_time, memory_time) with memory cost scaling as sum of context lengths, not batch count. This richer model partially explains the concave ITL growth — even without the batch cap, ITL would not follow a pure 1/(1-rho) curve because the marginal cost delta varies with the batch composition.
